tldr: This study achieves hardware traversal and failure recovery on a 19.6 kg life-sized dual-arm robot performing brachiation without demonstration data, using a novel framework called WGRL that guides whole-body reinforcement learning solely via sparse end-effector waypoints.
hero_caption: A sequence of photos showing a life-sized dual-arm robot dynamically performing brachiation across 30 mm diameter round bars spaced 0.4 m apart. In an environment with no footholds whatsoever, it swings its body widely to reach the next bar.
overview:
In recent years, reinforcement learning has dramatically boosted the locomotion capabilities of quadrupedal and bipedal robots. However, these systems rely strictly on environments with footholds. In contrast, primates such as apes swing beneath overhead branches and vines, alternating arms in a gait called brachiation to move swiftly through airborne space where no ground exists. Achieving arm-based locomotion in robots would drastically expand their traversable workspace. Yet, because it demands dynamic whole-body coordination and extremely precise timing for grasping and releasing bars, realizing robust brachiation on human-scale robotic hardware has remained extraordinarily challenging.

Applying conventional reinforcement learning to brachiation runs into two major roadblocks. First, unlike walking, there is no established body of reward-design knowledge, nor are demonstration motions available for imitation learning tailored to hooked end-effectors. Second, because the feet never touch the ground, even a tiny mistake instantly causes a fall and terminates the episode, making it a high-risk task.

To overcome these difficulties, the authors propose a learning framework called Waypoint-Guided Reinforcement Learning (WGRL). Instead of providing whole-body reference trajectories, WGRL sparsely specifies only the key end-effector waypoints essential to the task to guide initial exploration, letting reinforcement learning discover the required whole-body joint coordination on its own. Furthermore, by pairing a task success reward that encourages forward progression with a mechanical energy reward that suppresses excessive swaying, and gradually relaxing waypoint constraints through curriculum learning, the method achieves both stability and agility.

In simulation, the policy maintained a high success rate exceeding 90% across monkey bars with randomized height and angle variations, as well as on unseen inclined and circular courses. It also spontaneously developed a recovery behavior, flexing and extending its arms to regain balance and retry after missing a grasp. Finally, through zero-shot transfer without any additional tuning on hardware, the physical dual-arm robot—measuring approximately 1.1 m in height and weighing 19.6 kg—successfully crossed the monkey bars without falling a single time.
contributions: Proposed Waypoint-Guided Reinforcement Learning (WGRL), a reinforcement learning method that induces non-linear, complex motions from sparse end-effector waypoints alone, without requiring demonstration data.
Systematically demonstrated that incorporating the approach angle into the waypoint-following reward alongside distance is essential for learning convergence and task success.

Designed a paired reward scheme consisting of a bar-reaching success reward for forward progression and a mechanical energy reward to suppress excessive swaying, achieving both forward drive and post-grasp damping stabilization.

Demonstrated highly robust brachiation with spontaneous recovery behaviors after missed grasps across unseen monkey-bar environments with geometric variations and on a life-sized physical dual-arm robot.

sections.heading: No footholds? Just swing! The challenge of arm-based robotics
sections.summary: While quadrupedal and bipedal robots have achieved remarkable progress, brachiation in environments without footholds has remained largely uncharted territory. Facing severe fall risks and a lack of imitation data that make reinforcement learning difficult, this work aims for a breakthrough by pairing sparse end-effector waypoints with whole-body RL.
sections.details:
When thinking of robotic locomotion, legged movement—walking, running, and even parkour—is standard. However, all these behaviors assume a ground surface where feet can make contact. In post-disaster debris where footholds have collapsed or within dense forest canopies, primate-style brachiation using arm swings becomes a crucial mode of traversal.

Prior brachiation studies relied primarily on model-based classical methods such as energy-based control and virtual holonomic constraints. Because these strategies depend heavily on model accuracy, their robustness to contact uncertainty and external disturbances is limited. More recently, reinforcement learning approaches have been explored, but most remain confined to simplified models or small robots in simulation; successful demonstrations on human-scale physical hardware have been exceedingly rare.

Reward design difficulty and fall risk are the primary obstacles preventing the use of standard reinforcement learning. Rewarding forward velocity as done in walking policies does not induce the complex, non-linear sequence of unhooking, swinging forward, and looping over the next bar. Moreover, because high-quality motion capture data tailored to custom hook-style end-effectors does not exist, imitation learning frameworks like DeepMimic cannot be used.

To solve this, the paper presents Waypoint-Guided Reinforcement Learning (WGRL). Starting from only a few end-effector waypoints, the authors demonstrate adaptation to geometric perturbations in simulation and zero-shot traversal on a life-sized dual-arm physical robot.

sections.heading: A 19.6 kg dual-arm robot and irregular monkey-bar setups
sections.summary: The setup uses a 5-DoF-per-arm robot mimicking an adult upper body (1093 mm tall, 19.6 kg) equipped with custom hook end-effectors. The monkey-bar environment features randomized bar spacing, height, and yaw angles to enhance adaptability to hardware.
sections.details:
The task requires the robot to traverse overhead round bars by releasing one hand, reaching forward, hooking onto the next bar, and hanging, repeating this alternating sequence with both arms to progress forward.

- Robot platform: Based on the open-source hardware "MEVITA," the platform is a life-sized dual-arm robot modeling an adult male upper body. It has a total height of 1093 mm and a total weight of 19.6 kg. The arms feature a rigid metallic link structure capable of handling dynamic loads, providing 5 degrees of freedom per arm (shoulder roll, pitch, yaw; elbow pitch; and wrist pitch).
- Hook-style end-effectors: Custom aluminum hooks are attached to the wrists for hanging from bars. Compared to the 30 mm bar diameter, the inner hook diameter is 60 mm, providing generous clearance. The geometry consists of a 180-degree semicircular arc and a straight shank. This design contributes significantly to passive tolerance against positional errors, as described later.
- Monkey-bar environment: In the standard setup, 30 mm diameter, 1200 mm long round bars are aligned horizontally at 400 mm intervals. To withstand real-world errors and disturbances, the simulation injects substantial random perturbations into each bar's position during training: up to $\pm$20 mm in spacing, up to $\pm$40 mm vertically, and up to $\pm$0.2 rad in yaw relative to the heading direction.

captions.F2: Appearance of the life-sized dual-arm robot used in experiments (left) and the structure of the hook end-effector attached to each wrist (right). With an inner diameter of 60 mm (spacious for the 30 mm bar diameter), the 180-degree circular arc and straight shank prevent disengagement even during violent swinging.

sections.heading: Sparse guidance meets energy rewards: Inside the WGRL framework
sections.summary: WGRL places five waypoints on the end-effector's sagittal plane to guide early exploration. It employs an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup, combining a bar-reaching task success reward with a mechanical energy reward that tames excessive swinging.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Policy Architecture and RL Environment
Training uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with an asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture that handles different observation spaces.
- Actor (policy network): Receives only hardware-accessible observations: joint positions and velocities, base-link orientation and angular velocity from the IMU, previous target joint positions, and a binary phase signal $s_{\mathrm{phase}}$ indicating which arm should swing (0 for left, 1 for right). The policy executes at 50 Hz, and its target joint positions are sent to a 200 Hz PD controller.
- Critic (value network): In addition to the actor's input, the critic receives privileged information unavailable on hardware—including the positions, orientations, and radii of the five nearest bars relative to the base link, along with past histories of joint and IMU states—stabilizing value estimation during training.
- Simulation setup: Built on Legged Gym with 4096 parallel environments, applying domain randomization over friction coefficients, link masses, and center-of-mass positions.

### III-C Overview of Waypoint-Guided Reinforcement Learning (WGRL)
WGRL guides only key end-effector trajectories with a few sparse waypoints, allowing whole-body coordination to emerge freely through RL exploration. Five waypoints are defined in the 2D sagittal plane (longitudinal and vertical):
- $\boldsymbol{w}_1$: Moves the hook backward to clear the current bar, preventing it from jamming forward.
- $\boldsymbol{w}_2, \boldsymbol{w}_3$: Passes beneath the bar to move forward, avoiding collisions with the supporting bar.
- $\boldsymbol{w}_4, \boldsymbol{w}_5$: Elevates the hook high above the target bar and loops downward from behind onto it.
The waypoint threshold $\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{th}}$ begins at 0.03 and expands via curriculum learning as the passage rate across parallel environments increases. This enforces strict guidance early on, then loosens constraints to let natural whole-body dynamics take over.

### III-D & III-E Reward Design and Training Procedure
The WGRL reward combines a target waypoint position reward $r_{\mathrm{pos}}$, a progress reward $r_{\mathrm{prog}}$ based on rate of distance reduction, and a discrete success reward $r_{\mathrm{succ}}$ given upon arrival.
Crucial to the overall reward design is the pairing of a "Bars Reached" task success reward with a "Mechanical Energy" reward that regulates swinging. Mechanical energy is computed as the sum of translational kinetic energy and potential energy of the base link, tracking a stable reference value $e_{\mathrm{ref}}=-72\,\mathrm{J}$ corresponding to a stationary two-handed hang. This produces crisp motion dynamics: swinging vigorously forward to reach the next bar, then shedding excess energy immediately after grasping to settle the oscillation. Training runs for an initial 4000 iterations with high WGRL weight to establish basic mechanics, followed by 9000 iterations where success and energy rewards dominate to refine the motion.

captions.F3: Waypoint layout for the end-effector designed in WGRL. The three-stage guidance trajectory—(1) clearing the bar backward ($w_1$), (2) swinging forward under the supporting bar ($w_2, w_3$), and (3) lifting above the target bar to hook from behind ($w_4, w_5$)—induces complex hooking motions without demonstration data.

sections.heading: Lost without direction? Testing waypoint reward formulations
sections.summary: The authors evaluated four formulations for the waypoint position reward $r_{\mathrm{pos}}$ alongside combinations of the three WGRL reward terms. Constraining approach angle in addition to distance, as well as pairing continuous feedback with discrete success rewards, proved essential for successful learning.
sections.details:
To evaluate how the position reward $r_{\mathrm{pos}}=\operatorname{f}(\cos\theta,\tilde{\ell})$ affects training efficiency, four reward field formulations were compared. Here, $\tilde{\ell}$ is normalized distance, and $\theta$ is the angle between the vector from the prior waypoint to the target and the vector from the current position to the target.

- (a) Distance only $\exp(-\tilde{\ell}^2)$: Allowed broad exploration and started quickly (crossing an average of 0.5 bars in 1368 iterations), but easily fell into unhookable trajectories that collided from underneath, causing training to stall. Variance at 8000 iterations was high at 1.016, showing extreme instability.
- (b) Direction only $\cos\theta$: Provided insufficient incentive to close the distance, resulting in the worst performance with an average of only 0.257 bars reached at 8000 iterations.
- (c) Multiplicative combination $\cos\theta \cdot \exp(-\tilde{\ell}^2)$: Concentrated high rewards into a narrow region, achieving the fastest early progress (crossing 0.5 bars in 954 iterations) and the highest score at 8000 iterations with an average of 2.6 bars.
- (d) Additive combination $\cos\theta - 0.25\tilde{\ell}^2$: Applied a quadratic distance penalty even far from the target, stably pulling the hook toward the proper approach direction across a broad area. This wide-range guiding stability was selected as the standard configuration for subsequent experiments.

An ablation study across the position reward $r_{\mathrm{pos}}$, progress reward $r_{\mathrm{prog}}$, and success reward $r_{\mathrm{succ}}$ showed that removing the arrival check $r_{\mathrm{succ}}$ completely halted learning, while relying solely on sparse $r_{\mathrm{succ}}$ failed as well. Stable brachiation emerged only when all three terms worked in concert, uniting potential field guidance, temporal progress incentives, and explicit milestone completion.

captions.F4: Visualization of the reward field across four formulations of the position reward $r_{\mathrm{pos}}$: (a) distance only, (b) direction only, (c) multiplicative combination, and (d) additive combination. Arrows show the entry direction toward the target from the previous waypoint. As in (c) and (d), awarding high rewards only when approaching from the correct angle effectively narrows the search space.

sections.heading: Conquering unseen tracks and real hardware with self-recovery
sections.summary: In simulation, the policy crossed irregular courses as well as unseen sloped and circular tracks with over 90% success. It also transferred zero-shot to physical hardware, showing an emergent recovery behavior that built momentum to re-grasp after missing a bar.
sections.details:
### V-A Sim-to-Sim Evaluation: Unseen Environments and Recovery Behaviors
Simulation tests in the MuJoCo physics engine demonstrated remarkable policy robustness.
- Geometrically perturbed environments: Across courses with vertical variations of $\pm$40 mm and yaw variations of $\pm$0.2 rad, the policy completed 30 or more consecutive bars in all 10 trials. Crucially, a failure recovery behavior emerged: when the hook missed a bar, the robot rapidly flexed and extended the elbow of its supporting arm to absorb body oscillations, preventing a fall while swinging again to secure the bar.
- Unseen course profiles: On tracks not present during training, the policy achieved a 93.3% success rate (28/30 bars) on an undulating course with 5-degree slopes, and 91.0% (91/100 bars) on a circular course with 36 radially arranged bars.
- How does it adapt without cameras or external sensors? The policy observation includes no absolute bar coordinates or visual inputs. This robustness stems from the synergy between the looping hook trajectory discovered via WGRL and the mechanical passive tolerance of the hook shank, which slides into place upon contact. Additionally, the balanced trade-off between the fall penalty and the bar-reaching reward leads the policy to conclude that retrying a swing is far better than falling, naturally giving rise to recovery motions.

### V-B Hardware Verification: Zero-Shot Monkey-Bar Traversal
The policy trained in simulation was deployed directly to the physical robot without fine-tuning, traversing four bars spaced 400 mm apart.
On hardware, slight hook slips caused an initial miss due to friction differences from simulation. Yet, exactly as seen in simulation, the robot did not fall; supporting itself on one arm, it incrementally amplified its swing amplitude and securely caught the bar on its second attempt with greater momentum. It completed all three phases (right, left, right) and crossed the entire setup without falling.
Tracking the base link's mechanical energy revealed that kinetic energy peaks increased in steps during missed attempts to extend reach, and dropped sharply back to the reference value ($-72\,\mathrm{J}$) once two-handed support was restored, settling the robot into a resting state.

captions.F7: Traversal experiments across unseen environments in the MuJoCo simulator (Sim-to-Sim): (α) a degraded environment with perturbed bar positions and angles, (β) an undulating course with 5-degree slopes, and (γ) a radially arranged circular course. The lower plot traces base-link position over time, demonstrating steady forward progress without visual sensing.
captions.F8: Photo sequence of zero-shot brachiation on the life-sized dual-arm robot. Across bars spaced 400 mm apart, the robot alternates reach attempts—right arm (1–3), left arm (4–7), and right arm (8–10)—recovering from missed grasps by repeated swinging and completing the course without falling.

sections.heading: Opening new frontiers for robotic locomotion with arms
sections.summary: By combining sparse end-effector waypoints with reinforcement learning (WGRL), the authors realized robust brachiation on a life-sized robot without demonstration data. Future work aims to tackle irregular 3D environments by enforcing bilateral symmetry and integrating vision.
sections.details:
This paper realized brachiation control on a life-sized dual-arm robot through WGRL, which scaffolds early exploration using sparsely defined end-effector waypoints while letting reinforcement learning discover whole-body motions autonomously.

By integrating a potential reward combining distance and approach angle with progress and discrete success rewards, the policy naturally acquired a highly non-linear trajectory that unhooks and swings over bars from above. Furthermore, pairing forward-driving reach rewards with mechanical energy tracking produced an advanced whole-body strategy: dynamically amplifying swings after a miss, and promptly damping energy to stabilize once grasped.

This research provides clear, actionable design principles for reinforcement learning that expand the operational workspace of robots into environments devoid of footholds. Future directions include introducing symmetry constraints to resolve the left-right motion asymmetry observed in training, as well as incorporating visual sensors such as cameras to navigate irregularly placed bars and complex 3D obstacles.

takeaways: Even for challenging contact-rich, non-linear tasks lacking demonstration data, providing a few sparse end-effector waypoints allows reinforcement learning to autonomously discover coordinated whole-body motions.
When designing waypoint-following rewards, adding an approach angle vector constraint alongside scalar distance is critical to prevent search-space explosion and avoid local minima.
Pairing high-gain task success rewards against a target mechanical energy tracking reward enables spontaneous transitions between dynamic swing amplification and rapid post-grasp damping.
Combining passive mechanical tolerance from hook geometry with emergent recovery behaviors driven by severe fall penalties enables successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without vision sensors.
limitations: Learning convergence rates differed between the left and right movement phases, leaving noticeable asymmetry in the cycle period and swing amplitude between left- and right-arm reaches on hardware.
The system lacks visual sensors such as cameras or LiDAR to detect bar positions or thicknesses, preventing it from handling bars placed in completely unexpected locations.
A gap between the capsule-based contact approximation in simulation and the lower-friction contact on physical hardware caused frequent hook slips on initial reaching attempts on the real robot.
